item.text:
Based solely on the supplied text, these are the drafting vulnerabilities I would flag. Some are direct loopholes; others create enforcement uncertainty or litigation risk, rather than necessarily defeating the Act.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)—“Secretary” is undefined.** The bill does not identify who makes capability determinations; references elsewhere to Commerce and the Secretary of State do not resolve this expressly. That leaves the official responsible for a central element of the prohibition unspecified.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” permits fragmented training.** Companies could divide work among pretraining, continued training, fine-tuning, distillation, or separate component models and argue that no individual run exceeds the threshold. There is no aggregation rule for a coordinated development effort.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Training compute excludes other capability-producing computation.** The definition does not expressly count inference-time computation, search, synthetic-data generation, or other work outside training. Systems built with those methods could remain outside the automatic threshold unless separately designated under § 2(1)(B).

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—The threshold is fixed despite technical progress.** Algorithmic efficiency could allow increasingly capable models to be trained below \(10^{26}\) operations. There is no mechanism for updating the compute threshold, leaving coverage dependent on individual capability determinations.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** The bill supplies no rules for counting operations, including mixed-precision calculations, sparse computation, or multiply-accumulate operations. Different accounting methods could yield different coverage decisions and complicate proof.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Alternative computing methods may escape the metric.** The text counts only integer or floating-point operations and provides no equivalence rules for analog, optical, or other computation not naturally expressed that way. Developers could contest whether such computation counts at all.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Greater than” excludes the boundary.** A model trained using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is not automatically covered. Measurement uncertainty also creates room to dispute whether a model just above the line actually crossed it.

8. **§ 2(1)—“Model” and “system” have no defined relationship.** Subparagraph (A) covers models, while subparagraph (B) covers systems. The text does not explain coverage of ensembles, agents, tool-augmented systems, or products incorporating a covered model.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Capability coverage requires an affirmative determination.** A below-threshold system that actually exceeds human capabilities is not covered by this prong until the Secretary determines that it does. There is no mandatory assessment trigger, decision deadline, or interim restriction while evaluation proceeds.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is materially ambiguous.** “Substantially,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, reference populations, or measurement rules. Those uncertainties create fair-notice problems, especially when designation determines exposure to criminal punishment.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—The breadth requirement misses narrower dangerous capabilities.** A system with exceptionally dangerous capabilities in a few domains could fail the requirement to exceed humans across “most” cognitive tasks. Below the compute threshold, such a system could remain lawful despite presenting catastrophic risks.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—Evaluation conditions are unspecified.** The bill does not say whether capability is assessed with tools, scaffolding, additional inference compute, or safeguards removed. Companies could argue that a restricted deployment configuration controls even when the underlying system can perform substantially more powerful tasks.

13. **§ 2(1)(B)—Designation procedures and legal effect are missing.** There are no specified requirements for notice, evidence, publication, effective dates, reconsideration, or treatment of successor versions. Although ordinary administrative-law rules may apply, their application is left uncertain in a designation scheme carrying criminal consequences.

14. **§§ 2(1)(B), 3—The delegation invites avoidable constitutional challenges.** The Secretary receives substantial discretion to determine which systems become prohibited without detailed statutory criteria or procedures. That does not automatically invalidate the delegation, but clearer standards would reduce nondelegation and due-process litigation risk.

15. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” omits major categories of people and entities.** It excludes lawful permanent residents and other noncitizen U.S. residents when abroad, and does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or unincorporated organizations. Those omissions matter because § 3 relies on this definition for its overseas reach.

16. **§ 2(2)—Corporate coverage is geographically incomplete.** “Organized under the laws of a State” does not expressly include corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law. Such entities could contest whether they are covered when operating abroad.

17. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not covered merely because of U.S. ownership.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary or affiliate operating abroad is not itself a “U.S. person” under this definition. A U.S. parent's own prohibited conduct could still be reached, but ownership, control, or financing alone is not expressly prohibited.

18. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** There are no performance, bandwidth, interconnect, or other technical criteria for deciding which chips count. Operators could dispute coverage of general-purpose accelerators, custom hardware, or fewer but more powerful chips.

19. **§ 2(3)—The facility threshold permits physical and organizational fragmentation.** A site with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is excluded, and computing capacity can be spread across smaller sites. There is no aggregation rule for commonly controlled or interconnected facilities, although the underlying § 3 prohibition could still apply.

20. **§ 2(3)—Facility boundaries and chip-counting rules are unspecified.** “Data center” and “containing” do not establish whether adjoining buildings, campuses, colocated tenants, inactive equipment, or temporarily installed chips count together. Operators could structure or describe sites to avoid registration.

### Prohibited conduct and exemptions

21. **§§ 2(1)(A), 3(a)—Coverage during development is unclear.** A model is automatically covered because it was “trained using” more than the threshold, but the bill also prohibits its training and development. It does not clearly establish when a developing model becomes covered or prohibit starting a project expected to cross the threshold.

22. **§ 3(a)—The prohibited verbs are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” do not clearly distinguish research, testing, fine-tuning, hosting, operating, and using a system. Both enforcement and fair notice suffer if those boundaries must be established through penalty proceedings.

23. **§ 3(a)—Possession and transfers are not expressly prohibited.** The bill does not separately prohibit possessing covered model weights, distributing or selling them, exporting them, or releasing them openly. Some transfers might qualify as deployment, but relying on that interpretation leaves a significant gap.

24. **§ 3(a)—Facilitation and intermediary duties are not specified.** Providing compute, financing, technical assistance, or other support is not expressly addressed, nor are cloud providers given customer-verification or suspension duties. General criminal aiding-and-abetting and conspiracy doctrines may apply in appropriate cases, but do not replace a clear civil compliance regime.

25. **§ 3(a)—The location of remote conduct is unclear.** Cross-border cloud arrangements can separate the developer, servers, customers, and controlling entity. The bill does not specify where training or deployment occurs, or clearly address foreign operators supplying covered-system services into the United States.

26. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering is permanent and system-wide.** Any covered system whose training began before enactment is exempt from the entire prohibition, not merely allowed to finish its original training. The text therefore appears to permit continued development and deployment of grandfathered systems indefinitely, subject only to the Act's overall duration.

27. **§ 3(b)—A token training start could secure exemption.** “Training began” has no minimum substantive requirement. Companies could initiate many nominal runs before enactment and later claim that extensive development falls within the exemption.

28. **§ 3(b)—The identity of a grandfathered system is undefined.** The bill does not say when fine-tuning, architectural changes, new components, or successor versions create a new system rather than continue an old one. That permits arguments that substantially new capabilities inherit an earlier system's exemption.

29. **§ 3(b)—Grandfather claims need no documented approval.** There is no application, contemporaneous-record requirement, or designated process for verifying a claimed pre-enactment start. The bill also leaves proof burdens unclear, making questionable grandfather claims harder to resolve.

30. **§ 3(c)—The safety-evaluation exemption has no operational limits.** Any activity conducted “for the purpose of safety evaluation” is exempt, without limits on compute, system capability, duration, access, or deployment. A company could characterize substantial otherwise prohibited development as necessary to evaluate safety.

31. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose and self-certified evaluation are unresolved.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose, or require advance authorization or independent evaluators. Commercial development paired with some safety testing could therefore be claimed as exempt.

32. **§ 3(c)—Exempt evaluations lack containment and oversight requirements.** There are no mandatory security controls, incident reports, restrictions on releasing weights, or conditions governing outputs and follow-on use. Even genuinely safety-focused work could create or expose the capabilities the prohibition is intended to prevent.

### Registry and monitoring

33. **§ 4(a)—Registration has no deadline or update requirement.** Operators are told to register but not when, including whether registration must precede operations or follow threshold crossing within a specified period. Changes in ownership, capacity, or facility configuration need not expressly be reported.

34. **§ 4(a)—“Operator” and the registry's territorial reach are unclear.** The bill does not allocate responsibility among owners, tenants, cloud providers, and equipment managers, or specify whether foreign facilities must register. That creates both accountability gaps and jurisdictional disputes.

35. **§ 4(b)—Reporting attaches only to registered operators.** An operator that fails to register can argue that the quarterly-reporting obligation never attached. The reporting duty should not depend on compliance with the registration duty.

36. **§ 4(b)—Workload reports lack minimum content and timing rules.** “Describing” workloads does not require identifying customers, models, compute totals, linked runs, or claimed exemptions, and no submission deadline or certification standard is specified. Quarterly reporting also allows prohibited activity to proceed for months before routine disclosure.

37. **§§ 4–5—Registry violations have no express penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of § 3, not failures to register or report under § 4. Generally applicable laws may reach some false statements, but the bill lacks tailored sanctions for nonfiling, incomplete reports, or inaccurate certifications.

38. **§ 4—There are no express verification or record-retention powers.** The bill provides no audit, inspection, subpoena, telemetry, or records-preservation regime to test operator certifications. It also does not directly require developers outside covered facilities to preserve compute records or report potentially covered systems.

39. **§ 4—Sensitive reporting information lacks a tailored handling framework.** Workload disclosures may contain trade secrets, customer information, and security-sensitive details. Existing protections may apply, but the bill does not specify confidentiality, permissible sharing, or secure handling, inviting disputes over disclosure and agency use.

### Enforcement, penalties, and legal challenges

40. **§§ 3–5—Enforcement authority and procedures are incomplete.** The bill does not expressly assign civil investigation and enforcement responsibility or specify administrative assessment versus judicial recovery of penalties. Criminal prosecution has an ordinary federal pathway, but the civil regime should identify decisionmakers, procedures, and review.

41. **§§ 3–5—There is no express rapid intervention mechanism.** The text supplies no tailored authority to halt an ongoing training run, order a provider to suspend service, or obtain emergency relief. Generally available remedies may help, but penalties imposed afterward do not themselves stop dangerous activity.

42. **§§ 3–5—Post-violation disposition is unspecified.** The bill does not expressly provide for seizure, disabling, forfeiture, or secure disposition of unlawfully created models and related artifacts. Ending a training run or collecting a fine could leave the resulting capability available for later use.

43. **§ 5(a)—The civil cap may be an affordable cost of violation.** A maximum of $1 million per day is not tied to revenue, development expenditure, financial benefit, or repeat offending. There is no express disgorgement or higher penalty for deliberate circumvention.

44. **§ 5(a)—The unit and duration of a violation are unclear.** The text does not clearly establish whether multiple systems or prohibited acts generate separate daily penalties, or how partial days and continuing deployments are counted. Those ambiguities could materially limit recovery or produce inconsistent enforcement.

45. **§ 5—The civil and criminal knowledge standards need clarification.** Civil liability has no express mental-state requirement, while “willfully” does not specify what must be known about compute, designation, system capabilities, or illegality. Combined with vague definitions and exemptions, that creates both fair-notice concerns and proof problems.

46. **§§ 2–5—Extraterrestrial enforcement lacks supporting machinery.** Although § 3 expressly reaches U.S. persons abroad, the bill contains no tailored arrangements for obtaining overseas records, serving process, or securing foreign cooperation. Jurisdiction on paper will not ensure practical access to evidence or defendants.

47. **§§ 2–5—Constitutional fit is not addressed expressly.** To the extent “develop” or “deploy” reaches publication of code, weights, or scientific work, First Amendment challenges may arise; applications to purely intrastate, noncommercial activity could also generate federal-power disputes. Findings, clearer conduct definitions, and jurisdictional language would help address these issues, though their absence does not automatically make the bill unconstitutional.

48. **§§ 2–5, 8—Implementation authority and resources are missing.** The bill does not expressly authorize implementing regulations, set rulemaking deadlines, or provide dedicated resources for capability assessments, registry administration, and enforcement. Agencies may have some existing authority and funding, but the text leaves timely implementation uncertain.

### International provisions, duration, and commencement

49. **§ 6—The negotiation obligation has an ambiguous deadline and weak accountability.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly distinguish starting negotiations, pursuing them, or securing an agreement. There are no milestones or reporting requirements by which Congress could assess compliance.

50. **§ 6—“Equivalent” international prohibitions are underspecified.** The provision does not require common definitions, verification, enforcement, or restrictions on cross-border compute provision, and points only to § 3 rather than the registry and penalties. It could also be read to seek international replication of § 3's broad grandfathering and safety exemptions.

51. **§ 7(a)—The reopening standard is vague.** “Can be developed safely” does not specify acceptable risk, evidentiary requirements, deployment safety, or whether the finding concerns all covered systems or only some. The clause also leaves unclear whether a finding about a limited class would terminate the entire prohibition.

52. **§ 7(a)—The National Academies reporting process is not established.** No one is directed to commission or fund the report, and its scope, timing, independence safeguards, and public availability are unspecified. The joint resolution should also clearly state its operative legal effect and proceed through ordinary passage and presentment.

53. **§ 7(b)—The sunset overrides the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress has never found covered systems safe. Companies could simply wait out the prohibition, and the registry and enforcement framework would expire with it.

54. **§ 7—Post-termination administration is unresolved.** The text does not explain treatment of pending investigations, existing orders, retained records, or accrued liabilities after termination or expiration. General savings law may preserve some liabilities, but an express transition and savings provision would reduce disputes.

55. **§§ 5(a), 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) references violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act's effect for 180 days. Conduct before § 3 becomes operative ordinarily cannot violate it, so this mismatch invites disputes about retroactivity without clearly closing the gap.

56. **§§ 3(b), 8—The 180-day delay creates a development window.** Training begun after enactment is not grandfathered, but the prohibition does not take effect until day 180. Companies could accelerate training and distribute resulting artifacts during that interval; the bill imposes no interim controls or clear recall obligation.

57. **Act-wide—There is no severability clause.** A successful challenge to a central definition, exemption, or application could lead to litigation over how much of the remaining Act survives. Severability is not wholly dependent on an express clause, but stating Congress's intent would reduce that uncertainty.
